items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S9960

SPONSOR: MYRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the penal law, in relation to establishing the crimes of
benefiting from a sex trafficking venture and aggravated benefiting from
a sex trafficking venture; to amend the social services law, in relation
to establishing a right of action for victims of benefiting from a sex
trafficking venture; and to amend the civil practice law and rules and
the judiciary law, in relation to reviving such actions otherwise barred
by the existing statute of limitations, granting trial preference to
such actions, and directing the chief administrator of the courts to
promulgate rules for the timely adjudication of certain revived actions

 
PURPOSE:

An act to amend the penal law, in relation to establishing the crimes of
benefiting from a sex trafficking venture and aggravated benefiting from
a sex trafficking venture; to amend the social services law, in relation
to establishing a right of action for victims of benefiting from a sex
trafficking venture; and to amend the civil practice law and rules and
the judiciary law, in relation to reviving such actions otherwise barred
by the existing statute of limitations, granting trial preference to
such actions, and directing the chief administrator of the courts to
promulgate rules for the timely adjudication of certain revived actions.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Establishes the name of the bill: "the trafficking survivor
recovery and accountability act."

Section 2. Adds section 230.34-b to the penal law and defines: a sex
trafficking venture, persons benefiting from a sex trafficking venture,
persons participating in a sex trafficking venture, and persons giving
anything of value; makes benefiting from a sex trafficking venture a
class C felony.

Adds § 230.34-c to the penal law and defines aggravated benefiting from
a sex trafficking venture, sex trafficking venture, participating in a
sex trafficking venture, and persons giving anything of value; makes
benefiting from a sex trafficking venture a class B felony.

Section 3. Amends Subdivision (a) of section 483-aa of the social
services law. Adds victim of benefiting from a sex trafficking venture
from section 230.34-b and a victim of aggravated benefiting from sex
trafficking venture from section 230.34-c.

Section 4. Amends Paragraph (i) of subdivision (c) of section 483-bb of
the social services law. Defines "participates-in" for sex trafficking
ventures. Adds that the court may award additional punitive damages upon
a showing that the defendant's conduct was willful, wanton, reckless,
malicious, or in conscious disregard of the rights and safety of the
plaintiff; and the court may award punitive damages against the personal
representative, estate, successors, assignees, or distributees of a
deceased person held liable.

Section 5. Amends section 214-k which adds action certain victims of sex
trafficking can take when filing a claim.
Section 6. Amends paragraph 7 of subdivision (a) of rule 3403 of the
civil practice law and rules.

Section 7. Amends section 219-f which sets rules to reviving certain
action for the Chief Administrator of the courts.

Section 8 is the severability clause.

Section 9 is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

This bill modernizes New York's trafficking laws by amending the Penal
Law to create the crimes of benefiting from a sex trafficking venture
and aggravated benefiting from a sex trafficking venture, and by
conforming related remedial and procedural provisions so that survivors
have a meaningful path to recovery against those who knowingly benefit
from, participate in, or materially assist trafficking ventures. In
doing so, the bill is intended not merely to create a new civil remedy,
but to strengthen New York's criminal-law framework governing traffick-
ing and the enforcement mechanisms that flow from those offenses. The
bill also brings state law closer to the federal approach reflected in
18 U.S.C. § 1595, which permits a civil action not only against a direct
perpetrator, but also against one who knowingly benefits from partic-
ipation in a venture the person knew or should have known engaged in
trafficking.

The roots of barring punitive damages against estates lay not in legis-
lative, constitutional, or statutory action, but in common-law reasoning
that a claim is extinguished upon the death of the liable party. Yet in
other areas of New York law, including components of criminal and civil
forfeiture, civil rights, and consumer protection, liability is height-
ened or extended when a determination is made that society benefits from
such conduct being strongly deterred. Sexual abuse, trafficking, and
related sexual crimes fall squarely within that ambit, and New York law
should serve as both a shield of deterrence and sword of justice against
this abuse in all forms.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately
